title: The vendor bank change
brief: 16:34. An email from Ferrum Steel’s accounts team asks you to update their bank details before tonight’s payment run.
insight: Ferrum Steel is due £48,250 tonight. The email is from ferrum-steel’s accounts team, or so it says.
teaches: a bank detail change is checked on a number you already have
an email can come from a real supplier account and still be a scam
urgency before a payment run is a warning sign

pick: closing our old account for an audit
a merger with our parent company

choices.label: Did you email us to change your bank details?

script.say: Change our bank details? No, we have not sent anything like that. Our account has not changed. Please do not update it.

mail.subject: URGENT: bank details update before tonight’s payment
body: Please update our bank details before tonight’s run. Due to {{reason}} our old account is now closed and payments to it will bounce.
New sort code {{newSort}}, account {{newAcct}}, Northshore Bank. Confirm once done, this is time sensitive.

body.text: Update our details on our supplier portal

body.sign:
Gary Holt
Ferrum Steel Supply Ltd
Accounts

spf.explain: The message really was sent by {{fake.host}}. That is the attacker’s own domain, not Ferrum Steel’s, so SPF passing tells you nothing good here.

dkim.explain: Signed by {{fake.host}}, the sender’s domain. Again, that is the lookalike domain, not ferrumsteel.co.uk.

dmarc.explain: The From address matches the domain that signed it. The catch is that the domain is {{fake.host}}, not the real ferrumsteel.co.uk.

headers.summary: Every check passes because the attacker owns {{fake.host}} and set it up properly. The checks prove the domain sent it, not that the domain is who you think. Read the address: it is not ferrumsteel.co.uk.

replies.label: Reply: done, updated
replies.text: Done, I have updated your details.

replies.label: Reply: I will call to verify first
replies.text: Thanks, I will call your accounts line to verify before changing anything.

setup.title: Mail
setup.body: Ferrum Steel Accounts: URGENT bank details update

outcome.label: Read the full email headers
outcome.what: The checks pass because the attacker owns the lookalike domain. The headers show the message came from the lookalike, not from Ferrum Steel.
outcome.ideal: reads the headers and, more importantly, the sender domain, not just the display name.

outcome.label: Took out the vendor master file
outcome.what: The verified number for Ferrum Steel is 0114 496 0213. That is the number to call, not the one in the email.
outcome.ideal: checks the request against the independent record before acting.

outcome.label: Checked Ferrum Steel’s record in the ERP
outcome.what: The record shows the account on file and the verified phone number.
outcome.ideal: compares the request with the record on file.

outcome.label: Called Ferrum Steel back on the number on file
outcome.what: Gary confirms Ferrum Steel sent nothing and their account has not changed. That call is what breaks the fraud.
outcome.ideal: verifies a payment change by calling the number they already hold, never the number in the request.

outcome.label: Reported it to the service desk
outcome.what: The team can warn everyone and block the lookalike domain.
outcome.ideal: reports the attempt so others are warned.

outcome.label: Signed in on the fake supplier portal
outcome.what: The page at {{fake.host}} is not Ferrum Steel. Nothing you type there reaches them.
outcome.ideal: never signs in on a page a suspicious email linked to.

outcome.label: Replied to say it was done
outcome.what: The reply went to the attacker’s address, and nothing was actually verified.
outcome.ideal: does not confirm changes over the same email thread.

decide.step: Check the bank detail change before it goes through
decide.objective: Decide what to do with Ferrum Steel’s bank detail change (FS-4471 in Finance).
decide.insight: A genuine supplier would not lose their old account overnight, and a genuine change is verified by call back before it is used.

hint.text: Read the sender’s real address in Mail. Pull the vendor file from the drawer, call Ferrum Steel back on that number using the desk phone, then decide in Finance.

outcome.label: Approved the fraudulent bank change
outcome.what: Tonight’s £48,250 to Ferrum Steel now goes to the attacker’s account. By the time the real Ferrum Steel chases payment, the money is gone.
outcome.ideal: never approves a bank detail change without a call back to the number on file.

card.title: The money is gone
body: Finance sent tonight’s £48,250 to the new account. It was not Ferrum Steel’s. It was an account the attacker controls, emptied within the hour.
The one step that would have stopped it was a phone call to the number already on file, before changing anything.
card.ideal: verifies every bank change by calling the number on file, and never trusts the number or link in the request.
card.rewindLabel: Rewind to before I approved it

outcome.label: Rejected the change
outcome.what: The change is refused. Tonight’s payment goes to Ferrum Steel’s real account, the one already on file.
outcome.ideal: rejects an unverified change and keeps paying the account on file.

card.title: Caught before the run
body: You refused the change. Tonight’s payment goes where it always has, to Ferrum Steel’s real account.
The email address was a lookalike of ferrumsteel.co.uk. Every SPF and DKIM check passed, because the attacker owned the lookalike domain. The address bar and a phone call were what gave it away.
card.ideal: reads the real domain, verifies by call back, and rejects.

auto.text: Report it and learn from it.

hint.text: Raise a Helpdesk ticket so the team can try to recall the payment.
